title: ensemble-primer-velocity-lab-notes-noel
content:
Quick scratchpad for the "ensemble primer" velocity experiment. Notes to self / lab log; messy and partial.

Objective:
- Evaluate a lightweight multi-probe priming pattern ("ensemble primer") to reduce tail amplification for small-to-medium requests at bursty ingress. Want to keep p99 under SLO without huge batch inflation.

Hypothesis:
- Sending 3x short primer requests (10-40 tokens) spaced by 20-40ms before the real client request will: (a) warm attention kernels and KV-cache shards, (b) reduce cold-path JIT/alloc jitter, (c) increase hit rate for prefix edge-cases. Expect improvement in p95/p99 at cost of ~5-12% extra tokens.

Environment:
- Model: redwood-v2-slim-4b-quant (simulated production variant).
- Fleet: Dedicated A100-80GB pool, 8 GPUs, batcher configured with continuous batching (max_batch=64, timeout_ms=8).
- Runtime flags: kv_cache=on, prefill_fork=false, small-context-optimizer=enabled, adaptive-coalescer=off (turned off intentionally).
- Workload generator: custom wrk-like harness (python) that can emit sine-modulated QPS and per-request primer sequences.

Workload patterns and mixes:
- Baseline mix A: 80% small (<=32 tokens), 15% medium (33-128), 5% large (>128).
- Burst pattern: step from 50 QPS -> 1200 QPS over 7s, hold 30s, drop. Repeated every 6 min.
- New: ensemble-primer pattern: for each real request, send 3 primers: P1 (8 tokens), wait 25ms, P2 (18 tokens), wait 35ms, P3 (28 tokens), then main request. Primers marked with low-priority header so they can be de-duped on server side (experimental).

Runs and quick metrics (median of 3 runs each):
- Baseline (no primer) at burst peak 1200 QPS sustained for 30s:
  - observed throughput (per-GPU avg): ~145 qps
  - p50 end-to-end: 42ms
  - p95: 192ms
  - p99: 740ms
  - tail jitter: 30-45% over 1s windows
  - gpu util avg: 63%

- Ensemble-primer enabled (3 primers) same burst:
  - observed throughput (per-GPU avg): ~132 qps (-8.9%)
  - p50: 46ms (+9.5%)
  - p95: 118ms (-38.5%)
  - p99: 198ms (-73.2%)  << big win for p99
  - tail jitter: 12-18%
  - gpu util avg: 71% (higher due to primer tokens inflight)

- Ablation: 1 primer only:
  - p99: 420ms (mid improvement)
  - throughput: ~140 qps

- Ablation: increased primer spacing to 100ms (3 primers):
  - p99 improved slightly vs baseline but throughput dropped ~18% and p50 increased notably -> not acceptable.

Observations / interpretation:
- Ensemble primer tradeoff: costs ~8-10% throughput loss and extra token cost, but reduces p99 massively for bursty small-request mixes. This aligns with hypothesis that warming distributed KV shards and attention kernels avoids long cold tail events.
- The biggest win is at p99; p50 increased slightly but still within acceptable latency for most services.
- GPU utilization increases (more tokens processed), but occupancy is better (reduced stragglers).
- Spacing primers too long creates self-throttling; primers must be tight to be absorbed into same batching/coalescing epoch.
- Marking primers as low-priority allowed quick dropping in overload scenarios; need to verify server respects header everywhere (race with LB).
- Memory pressure: observed ephemeral spike in GPU mem allocations during first primer wave when many primed connections map to new KV shards. Peak +1.8GB per GPU; risk for very large models.

Telemetry notes:
- Trace correlation: primer span names prefixed with "primer.v1" -> helps identify warm vs real spans in APM.
- Added counter: primer_hit (true if primer caused non-empty KV hit on subsequent real request) -> ~62% primer_hit across runs (good).
- Need to instrument kernel JIT misses / kernel cache misses; currently not captured.

Quick checklist / next experiments:
- [ ] Try primers with adaptive length (start 8 tokens, bump if primer_hit low).
- [ ] Test primer header in private deployments (ensure KMS/proxy strips nothing).
- [ ] Run with adaptive-coalescer=on to see interaction (maybe better throughput with same p99).
- [ ] Explore "primer bloom" variant: single shared primer per GPU per 50ms slot that multiple clients piggyback on (lower token cost).
- [ ] Evaluate cost: approx token delta * 0.0009 $/1k tokens estimate -> rough cost impact for high-traffic customers.

Notes to product/PM: this pattern could be exposed as an optional client-side SDK mode ("velocity primer") or as a server-side auto-primer when request shape matches small-token-high-burst. Default behavior should be opt-in and gated by token-cost visibility.

Raw snippets (for reproducibility):
- wrk command: python harness --pattern step --qps 1200 --burst-duration 30 --primer "3,25,35" --mix small:0.8,medium:0.15,large:0.05 --model redwood-v2-slim-4b-quant
- perf counters: p99 extracted via probe with 100ms bins, bootstrap CI 95% reported.

Open questions / risks:
- Does primer increase side-channel info leakage? (primer shapes could be correlated to downstream content). Need security review.
- For very large models, memory spike may push us into OOM without additional buffer headroom. Not safe for >6B models without reservation.
- Client adoption friction: extra latency introduced by primers if network is high-latency. Need fallback to server-side warmers.

Conclusion (working):
- Ensemble primer looks promising as a pragmatic mitigation for p99 tail in bursty small request regimes. It is not free — throughput and token cost hit — but reduces worst-case by >70% in our tests. Worth follow-ups: adaptive primer sizing, server-side centralized primer, and production canary with low-priority primers only.

TODO immediate: push a small PR to runtime to expose primer header handling in the router and add a primer_hit counter. Then schedule a canary with customer A (non-sensitive workloads) for 2 weeks and monitor cost + p99.

End of notes. Will clean into a proper runbook if experiment repeats consistently across hardware/quantization variants.
